**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide whether to purchase additional local GPU hardware or to invest in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own. After several weeks of measurement, back-of-envelope modelling, and honest argument, we're recommending the second option: spend the next quarter improving utilisation before committing capital to new hardware. We want to lay out the reasoning, including where we could still be wrong.

Start with the economics. Our current fleet of eight A100-class cards runs at roughly 34% average utilisation, with peaks near 90% during training runs and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. That number is not unusual, but it means we are paying depreciation, power, and rack space for capacity that sits dormant most of the time. A new node would cost approximately £180k up front plus around £2k monthly in power and cooling, and lead times are currently eight to twelve weeks. By contrast, the utilisation work — a proper job scheduler, shared inference endpoints with batching, and a policy for checkpointing and releasing idle reservations — is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway, plus perhaps £15k for software licences and monitoring tooling. If we can lift average utilisation to 60%, we effectively add the equivalent of two to three cards of capacity without buying anything, and we keep the option to buy later with better information about our real demand curve.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and we take it seriously. Our interactive services currently share hardware with batch training jobs, and when contention occurs, p95 inference latency degrades from 180ms to well over a second. Buying dedicated inference hardware would solve this cleanly and immediately. But the diagnosis matters: the degradation is caused by unmanaged co-tenancy, not by absolute capacity shortage. Isolating inference onto two reserved cards and moving batch work onto the remainder would restore latency without new purchases, and it would also make our capacity planning more honest, because we would finally see the true demand for each workload class rather than a blended, noisy signal.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy: if a card fails today, we lose a sixth of our training capacity, and our single inference node is a genuine single point of failure. That risk is real and we should not minimise it. However, buying a second inference node before we understand our failure and demand patterns risks purchasing insurance against a problem we haven't quantified. The utilisation work includes better failure telemetry and a documented failover path, which reduces the blast radius of an outage at modest cost. If, after that, the reliability math still argues for redundancy, we will be in a far stronger position to specify exactly what to buy.

Opportunity cost deserves explicit mention. The £180k for a new node is not just money; it is roughly two engineer-quarters of hiring budget or the entire remaining allocation for our retrieval-quality project, which we believe will deliver more customer value than marginal training throughput. There is also an organisational opportunity cost: teams that know hardware is scarce tend to write leaner jobs and delete stale experiments. Scarcity, within reason, is a discipline. Abundance purchased before the discipline exists tends to be absorbed by inefficiency within a quarter — we have all seen this pattern elsewhere.

Reversibility is perhaps the decisive factor. Improving utilisation is cheap to reverse or redirect: if the scheduler work stalls, we have lost weeks, not capital. Buying hardware is largely irreversible at our scale; GPUs depreciate quickly, resale is friction-filled, and a purchase made on this quarter's demand pattern may fit poorly next year's. When one option preserves optionality and the other forecloses it, and both plausibly solve the problem, the reversible choice should win unless it is clearly inadequate. We do not believe it is.

To be clear about uncertainty: our utilisation figures come from three weeks of telemetry and may overstate idle capacity if recent demand is a leading indicator of sustained growth. If the product roadmap commits to two large training campaigns next quarter, our analysis changes materially, and we should revisit this in eight weeks with fresh numbers. We therefore propose a concrete checkpoint: implement the scheduler and workload isolation, re-measure, and bring a follow-up recommendation — including a specific purchase proposal if utilisation exceeds 70% or latency targets remain unmet — before the next budget cycle.

In short: the hardware we own is underused, the fixes are cheap and reversible, and buying now would spend money and optionality to avoid an engineering problem we are capable of solving. Let's solve it first.

We're happy to walk through the telemetry with anyone who wants to challenge the numbers — we would rather be argued out of this now than after a purchase order is signed.

appliance.hardware: 2 x NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10, 128 GB unified memory per appliance
appliance.kv_cache_layout: MLA latent fp8_g128 (8448 B per 16-token block per layer, 11 layers) + sparse-index cache (1024 B per block per layer + slot-mapped tails); 2 GiB of it in the GB10 display carveout
